Subject: Dedicated capacity requirements: long-context models (initial ask)

Hi Aditya,

Quick intro — I'm Emma (Head of ML Ops, TidalBio). We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated for hosting two production models:

- tidal-bio-70b (modified Llama-family) — target 64k context, primary inference for extractive question answering over clinical notes.
- tidal-summ-13b — target 32k context, faster summarization and reranking.

Expected traffic profile (first 6 months): average 150 QPS combined, 95th-percentile bursts ~600 QPS for short windows (1–5m) during batch ingestion. Typical hot session lengths: 2–8k tokens; cold retrieval flows occasionally require full 64k KV walk.

Questions we need answered for procurement:
1) GPU/reserved pool sizing to meet latency SLO (95th < 300ms for tidal-summ, < 600ms for tidal-bio at 64k when not doing full retokenization).
2) Impact of 4-bit / int8 quantization on memory footprint and throughput — what are safe defaults you recommend for production?
3) KV cache memory sizing assumptions per concurrent session and options for shared KV caching to lower GPU RAM needs.
4) How autoscaling/burst capacity would work for short 600 QPS spikes if we reserve a smaller base pool.

We have some compliance constraints — all inference must remain in our VPC (Private deployment) and we want to lock pricing for the first 12 months. Can you produce a short dedicated-capacity plan + cost ballpark and a mutual action plan?

Thanks,
Emma
Emma Carter
Head of ML Ops, TidalBio

Emma — thanks for the clear brief. Looping in Lauren (runtime sizing) and Marcus (KV/cache & perf) for a technical pass; Stephanie will scope procurement/pricing.

High level: we can support both models in a Dedicated Private deployment inside your VPC. Early takeaways that we'll validate with perf runs:
- Quantization: 4-bit (AWQ/QLoRA style) typically reduces GPU memory footprint 2.5–3x vs fp16 with minimal quality loss for many Llama-family weights; int8 can be a good compromise for latency-critical paths. We'll call out per-model guidance.
- KV cache: full 64k contexts imply large KV state; we can use per-request prefix caching + shared (cold) KV backing store to reduce active GPU RAM. Marcus will share numbers.
- Autoscale: recommended base reserved pool sized for 95th steady-state, with burst pool (on-demand) to handle short spikes. We'll propose base vs burst counts and expected cold-start latencies.

Attached is a first-pass capacity spreadsheet (tidal_capacity_matrix.csv) with conservative numbers; Lauren/Marcus — please update with model-specific memory rows + recommended reserved GPU counts and per-GPU concurrency.

Next steps: internal sizing update by EOD tomorrow (Lauren), then I'll produce a customer-facing capacity + price summary.

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity requirements: long-context models (technical sizing)

Emma / team — technical sizing notes after running perf baselines and model mem estimates (summary). I'm including the model_memory_breakdown.pdf in attachments (pdf stub).

Assumptions used:
- Model weights: tidal-bio-70b (fp16 baseline ~140 GB), tidal-summ-13b (fp16 baseline ~26 GB).
- KV cache: KV per token ~0.45 bytes/token per key-value element after compression in our runtime; practical working KV requires overhead (indices, segments) — we use 0.7x multiplier for safety.
- Target latencies: median <150ms, p95 <600ms for tidal-bio at long context if KV is cached. For cold full-KV walks p95 may degrade to ~1s without prewarming.

Memory footprints (per-GPU) — rough guidance:
- tidal-bio-70b:
  - fp16: ~140GB weights + 64k KV active (worst-case) ~48GB => not feasible on single 80GB GPU; requires model sharding (tensor parallel) across GPUs.
  - int8: weights ~75GB; 4-bit AWQ: ~32–40GB effective weights. With 4-bit + offloadable KV we can fit model shards on 2x H100 80GB with optimized kernels; recommended 4-way tensor-parallel spread across 4x H100 for headroom and throughput.
- tidal-summ-13b:
  - fp16: ~26GB weights; int8: ~14GB; 4-bit: ~6.5–8GB. Sufficient to run 2–3 concurrent shards on a single H100 depending on KV footprint.

Concurrency and GPU counts (reserved base pool recommendations):
- Base (steady 95th ~200–250 QPS):
  - tidal-bio-70b: 8x H100 nodes (with model sharding 4-way TP per request, effective concurrency ~8–12 reqs/node depending on batch). This yields ~250 QPS steady under our measured microbenchmarks for 32k avg seq.
  - tidal-summ-13b: 2x H100 nodes dedicated (or colocated with headroom on the same fleet) for ~150 QPS.
- Burst capacity (on-demand) for short spikes to 600 QPS: ephemeral pool of +10 H100s available via reserved-burst credits; warm-up time for new nodes ~30–90s depending on KV prewarm.

Quantization impact: 4-bit reduces model memory by ~2.5–3x and increases throughput 1.6–2x given optimized kernels; latency benefit is model-dependent. We recommend 4-bit AWQ for tidal-bio-70b for production if you validate on your eval sets. Keep int8 as fallback for any outlier prompts where quality/regression is observed.

KV strategies to lower GPU RAM need:
- Active per-conversation KV cache (~hot sessions) should be held in GPU memory only for top N hot sessions; cold KV can be kept on fast NVMe and streamed.
- Shared prefix caching: common clinical prefixes / tokenize-once segments cached in a shared in-memory store on dedicated nodes to avoid recomputing the same KV for similar prompts. This reduces active GPU KV by ~30–50% for our clinical datasets.

Operational recommendations:
- Start with 12x H100 reserved (base 10 + 2 buffer) and a burst pool of 10. This provides headroom for model sharding and rolling deploys.
- Or, if budget constrained, pilot with 8x H100 + aggressive 4-bit quantization and enable autoscale for bursts (we'll map expected cold-start latency).

I'll attach the detailed memory breakouts in model_memory_breakdown.pdf and update the tidal_capacity_matrix.csv with per-GPU concurrency rows.

— Lauren Bishop
Senior Runtime Engineer, Redwood Inference
